people.name: Marie Sokol Procai
people.field: Folk art, small business, community building
body: In the early 1910s a Ukrainian teenager named Marie Sokol stepped off a train in Minneapolis. She was on her way to Winnipeg, Canada. In Minneapolis she found her own cousin already living there, and she stayed. By the family's account she was born in Dobrochyn, in the Sokal region, grew up partly in Yugoslavia, and at 14 crossed the ocean alone through Ellis Island to join a brother on a Pennsylvania farm. The Banner puts her arrival in America at 13.

Northeast Minneapolis was already home to Ukrainian immigrants. MNopedia dates the community to the late 1870s. Many early arrivals were laborers from villages under the rule of other empires, and many men worked in the mills, where rents nearby were low enough for working families to put down roots. St. Constantine Ukrainian Catholic Church was founded in 1913, and St. Michael's Ukrainian Orthodox Church formed in 1925.

In 1915 Marie married Tony Procai, also a Ukrainian immigrant, and the couple helped build Ukrainian community life in the city. She also carried pysanky with her, Ukrainian Easter eggs decorated with a wax-resist method: each line is drawn in beeswax and the egg goes through dye baths from light colors to dark. In Minneapolis she worked with the tools and dyes she could find in America.

In November 1947 Marie and her daughter Luba opened a small gift shop in the Procai living room, selling embroidery, ceramics, books and other goods. In April 1972 National Geographic ran an eight-page pictorial that featured the shop, the Minneapolis Ukrainian community and the art of pysanky. The family says she worked six days a week until she retired at 90, in 1987.

Her publisher's page and The Banner say she died in 1994. The family shop's history says 1993. Her story reached a new generation in 2026 with Marie's Magic Eggs, a children's picture book by Sandra Neil Wallace and Evan Turk.
keyFacts: Early 1910s: Arrived in Minneapolis on the way to Winnipeg, and stayed after finding her cousin there.
1915: Married Tony Procai.
November 1947: Opened the Ukrainian Gift Shop with her daughter Luba, in the family living room.
April 1972: National Geographic pictorial featured the shop and pysanky.
1987: Retired at 90.
2026: Subject of the picture book Marie's Magic Eggs.

people.name: Luba Perchyshyn
body: For decades, people across the country learned to make Ukrainian Easter eggs from a kit packed in Minneapolis. The woman behind those kits was Luba Perchyshyn, born Luba Procai in the United States to Ukrainian immigrant parents, Marie and Tony Procai.

In November 1947 she and her mother opened a gift shop in the family living room. On opening day they sold two handkerchiefs for $1.50. The shop soon moved to a store near the University of Minnesota, and there Luba put together her first egg-decorating kit, tools, dyes and wax in a paper bag, for one dollar. Her sister Johanna Luciow joined the business in 1958 and added her own pysanky artistry.

Refined versions of the kits are now sold internationally. A 1975 film, Pysanky, by Slavko Nowytski featured her egg decorating and won an International Gold Eagle Award in 1978. The family has published a series of pysanky design books, including Ukrainian Easter Eggs and How We Make Them (1979).

The Star Tribune profiled her in 2015, at 91. She lived with dementia in her last years and spent her last months at Catholic Eldercare in Northeast Minneapolis, in the family's words, treasured by the staff and her family. She died on September 7, 2020, at 96. Her son Elko now manages the business, which by its own account no longer has a walk-in showroom and sells online.
keyFacts: 1923: Born to Ukrainian immigrant parents; the year is worked out from her age in 2015 and 2020.
November 1947: Opened the shop with her mother.
First kit: tools, dyes and wax in a paper bag, one dollar.
1975: Featured in Slavko Nowytski's film Pysanky.
September 7, 2020: Died in Minneapolis at 96.

people.name: Alexander A. Granovsky
body: After World War II, a University of Minnesota professor traveled to the displaced persons camps of Europe. Alexander Granovsky met with Ukrainians there and recruited people, especially skilled workers, for jobs in the Twin Cities. MNopedia says hundreds accepted. That wave reshaped the Ukrainian community in Minneapolis and St. Paul.

Granovsky was born on November 4, 1887, in Berezhtsi in the Volhynia region, then part of the Russian Empire. As a young man he was a modernist poet whose work appeared in Kyiv journals. He studied at the Kyiv Commercial Institute in 1909 and 1910, emigrated to the United States in 1913, and earned a PhD at the University of Wisconsin in 1926.

He taught entomology and economic zoology at Wisconsin and then for many years at Minnesota. He became a world authority on aphids, and two species were named after him. He did pioneering work on how insects spread plant diseases and, by the Encyclopedia of Ukraine's account, was the first U.S. entomologist to run large-scale field tests of DDT against potato insects.

He was also a national Ukrainian American leader. He was president of the Organization for the Rebirth of Ukraine from 1935 to 1963, published Ukraine's Case for Independence in 1940, and helped found the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America. He died in St. Paul in 1976.

1913: Emigrated to the United States.
1926: PhD, University of Wisconsin.
After World War II: Recruited displaced Ukrainians for jobs in the Twin Cities.
1935–1963: President of the Organization for the Rebirth of Ukraine.
1976: Died in St. Paul.

people.name: Bronko Nagurski
body: Bronko Nagurski is one of the best-known names in Minnesota sports. He was born on November 3, 1908, in Rainy River, Ontario, across the border from International Falls, and moved to International Falls at about four. His parents came from Galicia, a region of Austria-Hungary now split between western Ukraine and southeastern Poland.

Sources disagree on his heritage. EBSCO's biography says his parents were from Ukraine, other accounts say Ukrainian and Polish, and the Polish-American Sports Hall of Fame claims him as Polish. His story shows why a birthplace or an old record cannot settle how a family identified.

At the University of Minnesota he was an All-American at both fullback and tackle, and he entered the College Football Hall of Fame in 1951. He played for the Chicago Bears from 1930 to 1937, with five All-NFL selections and titles in 1932 and 1933. He left in 1938 and turned to professional wrestling, which he kept up until 1960, holding the National Wrestling Alliance world title several times. He returned to the Bears in 1943 and scored the go-ahead touchdown in that year's title game.

In 1963 he joined the Pro Football Hall of Fame as a charter member, and the Bears retired his No. 3. The Football Writers Association of America has given a national defensive award since 1993, and named it for him in 1995. He ran a gas station in International Falls until 1968 and died there on January 7, 1990, at 81.
keyFacts: November 3, 1908: Born in Rainy River, Ontario.
University of Minnesota All-American at fullback and tackle.
1930–1937 and 1943: Chicago Bears, with NFL titles in 1932, 1933 and 1943.
1938–1960: Professional wrestling.
1963: Charter member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
January 7, 1990: Died in International Falls.
people.connectToWork: Where do your forms or records force one ancestry or nationality on someone whose family history crossed changing borders, and what would you ask instead?

people.name: Wasyl and Anna Kramarczuk
people.dates: Arrived in the United States in the late 1940s
body: At 215 East Hennepin Avenue in Minneapolis, a sausage shop has drawn customers for generations. Kramarczuk's was started by Wasyl and Anna Kramarczuk, who came from the village of Pidhajci and arrived in the United States in the late 1940s, in the years when displaced Ukrainians were resettling after World War II.

Wasyl was a sausage maker, and Anna was a cook and baker. After years of hard work they opened their own business in Northeast Minneapolis. MNopedia says it thrived in the 1950s and 1960s. Others from Pidhajci settled nearby, among them Dmytro Mandybur, who founded a Ukrainian credit union and in 1964 organized what became the Ukrainian American Community Center.

By the company's account it still makes its products by hand from scratch, and it won the James Beard Foundation's America's Classic award in 2013. Its sausages are sold at Target Field. MNopedia credits Kramarczuk's, the neighborhood's churches and the community center with making Ukrainians one of the most visible European immigrant groups in Minneapolis. The James Beard Foundation says Wasyl Kramarczuk died in 1991 and Anna Kramarczuk in 2008, and that the business dates to 1954, when they bought Central Provisions. Orest Kramarczuk told KSTP his parents came to the United States in 1949.
keyFacts: Late 1940s: Came to the United States from Pidhajci.
Wasyl was a sausage maker, and Anna was a cook and baker.
1950s–1960s: The business grew in Northeast Minneapolis.
2013: James Beard America's Classic award, by the company's account.
215 East Hennepin Avenue, Minneapolis.

people.name: Igor Sikorsky
body: On September 14, 1939, in Stratford, Connecticut, Igor Sikorsky climbed into an open frame of steel tubing with a single large rotor overhead and a small rotor on its tail. The VS-300 rose a few feet off the ground, and its layout is the one most helicopters still use.

Sikorsky was born in Kyiv on May 25, 1889, when Kyiv was part of the Russian Empire. While a student at the Kyiv Polytechnic Institute he built two helicopters, in 1909 and 1910. From 1912 to 1917 he was chief designer at the Russian-Baltic aviation works, where he built the Grand, the world's first successful four-engine airplane, in 1913, and more than 70 Ilya Muromets planes that served as bombers in World War I.

After the 1917 revolution he left for France and then the United States, reaching New York at the end of March 1919. In 1923 he founded the company that became Sikorsky Aircraft, and he became a citizen in 1928. Its flying boats opened transoceanic airline service in the 1930s. The XR-4, delivered in 1942, was the first production helicopter, and the R-4 from 1943 was the first built in large numbers.

He received the Guggenheim Medal in 1951 and the National Medal of Science for 1967. He died in Easton, Connecticut, on October 26, 1972. Sources describe him differently: the San Diego Air and Space Museum calls him Russian-American, and the Encyclopedia of Ukraine includes him as Ihor Sikorsky.
keyFacts: May 25, 1889: Born in Kyiv.
March 1919: Arrived in New York.
1923: Founded the company that became Sikorsky Aircraft.
September 14, 1939: First flight of the VS-300.
1942–1943: The XR-4 and R-4 became the first production helicopters.
October 26, 1972: Died in Easton, Connecticut.

people.name: Alexander Archipenko
body: In 1933, visitors to Chicago's Century of Progress fair walked into the Ukrainian pavilion and found 44 works by Alexander Archipenko. By then he was known as one of the artists who brought Cubism into sculpture, often using open spaces as part of the form.

Archipenko was born in Kyiv on May 30, 1887. He studied at the Kyiv Art School from 1902 to 1905 and was expelled for criticizing his teachers. By the Archipenko Foundation's chronology he reached Paris in 1909, left the École des Beaux-Arts after about two weeks and set up a studio in Montparnasse. He showed with the Cubists from 1910 and opened his own school in 1912.

He moved to the United States in 1923 and ran schools in New York, Woodstock and Chicago. The foundation dates his citizenship to 1929, while the Smithsonian says 1928. He experimented with painted reliefs he called sculpto-paintings and, in the late 1940s, carved plastic lit from within.

Many of his works took Ukrainian subjects, including busts of the poet Taras Shevchenko. In 1962 he was elected to the National Institute of Arts and Letters. He died in New York on February 25, 1964. The Encyclopedia of Ukraine says recognition in Ukraine began only in the late 1980s.
keyFacts: May 30, 1887: Born in Kyiv.
1912: Opened an art school in Paris.
1923: Moved to the United States.
1933: 44 works at the Ukrainian pavilion in Chicago.
1962: Elected to the National Institute of Arts and Letters.
February 25, 1964: Died in New York.
people.connectToWork: When a person's history was erased or left out of official records at home, what could your intake or records miss, and how would you make room for their own account?

people.name: Jack Palance
body: At the 1992 Academy Awards, 73-year-old Jack Palance accepted the Oscar for Best Supporting Actor for City Slickers. Decades earlier he had been a coal miner's son in Pennsylvania named Volodymyr (Walter) Palahniuk.

He was born on February 18, 1919, in Lattimer Mines, Pennsylvania, to Ukrainian immigrant parents, and worked in the mines with his father as a boy. He boxed professionally in the late 1930s as Jack Brazzo. He enlisted in the Army Air Forces in 1942 and became a bomber pilot. During a training flight over Arizona his B-24 caught fire and he parachuted out, with injuries that needed surgery. He was discharged in 1944.

He graduated from Stanford on the GI Bill in 1947, understudied Marlon Brando in A Streetcar Named Desire on Broadway, and made his film debut in Panic in the Streets (1950). Academy Award nominations followed for Sudden Fear (1952) and Shane (1953). He appeared in more than 50 films and spoke some Ukrainian on screen in Bagdad Café (1988). He changed Palahniuk to Palance after the war.

On April 22, 2004, at a Russian Nights festival gala in West Hollywood, he was to receive a Russian honor. By published accounts he said that he was Ukrainian, not Russian, and walked out. He died at his daughter's home in Montecito, California, on November 10, 2006.
keyFacts: February 18, 1919: Born in Lattimer Mines, Pennsylvania.
1942–1944: Army Air Forces bomber pilot, injured when his B-24 caught fire.
1950: Film debut in Panic in the Streets.
1992: Oscar for City Slickers.
April 22, 2004: Refused a Russian honor at a West Hollywood gala.
November 10, 2006: Died in Montecito, California.
people.connectToWork: A changed or anglicized name can hide a family's history. How do your systems hold a person's preferred name, legal name and earlier names without treating any as a mistake?

people.name: Mary V. Beck
body: In 1950, by the Encyclopedia of Detroit's account, Detroit voters elected a woman to the City Council for the first time. Mary Beck, a lawyer and the daughter of Ukrainian immigrants, served for 20 years. The Ukrainian American Archives and Museum of Detroit dates her service from 1949.

Beck was born on February 29, 1908, in Ford City, Pennsylvania. She earned a law degree at the University of Pittsburgh in 1932 and moved to Detroit about two years later. She spent a year as a social worker at the International Institute, which served immigrants, worked as a juvenile court investigator for Wayne County from 1934 to 1947, and was admitted to the Michigan bar in 1944.

She became the first woman to serve as the council's president pro tempore and then as its president, and she sat on the Wayne County Board of Supervisors. She founded the Ukrainian Women's Literary Award and was an officer of the Detroit branch of the Ukrainian National Women's League of America.

She retired in 1970. She entered the Michigan Women's Hall of Fame in 1991, and in 2003 the Ukrainian World Congress gave her its St. Volodymyr Medal. She died on January 30, 2005, at 96, in Clinton Township, Michigan.

1932: Law degree, University of Pittsburgh.
1934–1947: Juvenile court investigator, Wayne County.
Elected to the Detroit City Council and served until 1970.
1991: Michigan Women's Hall of Fame.
January 30, 2005: Died at 96.

people.name: Mila Kunis
body: In March 2022, days after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, actor Mila Kunis and her husband Ashton Kutcher started an online fundraiser for people fleeing the war, matching up to $3 million of donations. By March 18 it had passed its $30 million goal. On March 20 President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly thanked the couple, saying they had raised $35 million, which went to Flexport and Airbnb to ship supplies and house refugees.

Kunis was born Milena Kunis on August 14, 1983, in Chernivtsi, then in the Ukrainian SSR. She grew up in a Jewish family and has said her whole family was in the Holocaust. In 1991, when she was seven, the family moved to Los Angeles, seven people with suitcases and $250. She has named antisemitism in the Soviet Union as one reason they left. Her father, a mechanical engineer, drove a cab and her mother, a physics teacher, worked in a drugstore after learning English.

She has said she cried every day in second grade, not understanding the language. At 14 she was cast as Jackie Burkhart on That '70s Show, which ran until 2006. She voices Meg Griffin on Family Guy, and Black Swan (2010) earned her a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination. By Biography.com's account she speaks Russian with her parents.
keyFacts: August 14, 1983: Born in Chernivtsi.
1991: Moved to Los Angeles at seven.
2010: Screen Actors Guild Award nomination for Black Swan.
March 2022: Co-founded a refugee fundraiser that raised $35 million.
people.connectToWork: Someone born in Ukraine may be Jewish, may speak Russian at home, or both. Which of your forms assume that country, language and identity go together, and what would you ask instead?

people.name: George Kistiakowsky
body: In July 1945, in the New Mexico desert, George Kistiakowsky watched the Trinity test, the first explosion of a nuclear weapon. As head of the Explosives (X) Division at Los Alamos, he had led the work on the explosive lenses that squeezed the bomb's plutonium core.

He was born on November 18, 1900 (December 1 on the modern calendar), in Boyarka, near Kyiv, then part of the Russian Empire, into what the National Park Service calls an old Ukrainian Cossack family. During the civil war he fought in the anti-Bolshevik White Army. In 1920 he escaped on a commandeered French ship, going to Turkey, Yugoslavia and then Germany.

He earned a PhD in physical chemistry at the University of Berlin in 1925 and came to the United States in 1926, first to Princeton. He joined Harvard in 1930 and became professor emeritus in 1971. He was invited to the Manhattan Project in late 1943 and took over the X Division in January 1944.

He joined the President's Science Advisory Committee in 1957, and in 1959 President Eisenhower made him his Special Assistant for Science and Technology. In 1968 he broke his ties with the Pentagon to protest the Vietnam War. He received the Medal of Freedom in 1961 and the National Medal of Science for 1967. He died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on December 7, 1982.
keyFacts: November 18, 1900 (Old Style): Born in Boyarka, near Kyiv.
1920: Left after fighting in the civil war.
1926: Came to the United States.
1930: Joined the Harvard faculty.
1944–1945: Led the X Division at Los Alamos.
1959: Became Eisenhower's science adviser.
December 7, 1982: Died in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
people.connectToWork: A refugee's path can run through several countries before it reaches you. Where do your forms or timelines assume one straight move from home to here, and what does that miss?

people.name: Vladimir Horowitz
body: In 1986, after 61 years away, Vladimir Horowitz sat down at a piano in Moscow. The recital was televised internationally. He had left in 1925 on a six-month visa to study in Germany and had never gone back.

Horowitz was born on October 1, 1903, in Kyiv, then part of the Russian Empire, the youngest of four children in a musical Jewish family. His mother, a pianist, was his first teacher. He entered the Kyiv Conservatory in 1912 and began giving concerts in 1920, partly to help support his family. Some older sources name Berdychiv as his birthplace, but his birth certificate names Kyiv.

He made his American debut at Carnegie Hall on January 12, 1928, and settled in the United States. He played at a 1943 war bond rally that raised more than $10 million. He withdrew from the stage several times, once for 12 years, and his return to Carnegie Hall on May 9, 1965, sold out in two hours.

President Reagan presented him with the Presidential Medal of Freedom on July 28, 1986. Deutsche Grammophon counts 24 Grammy Awards, and Musical World counts 25. He died in New York on November 5, 1989, four days after his last recording session.

1925: Left the Soviet Union to study in Germany.
January 12, 1928: U.S. debut at Carnegie Hall.
May 9, 1965: Returned to the stage after 12 years.
1986: Recitals in Moscow and Leningrad.
July 28, 1986: Presidential Medal of Freedom.
November 5, 1989: Died in New York.

people.name: Oksana Baiul
body: At the 1994 Winter Olympics in Lillehammer, Norway, a 16-year-old skater from Ukraine edged out the American Nancy Kerrigan for the gold medal, by a 5–4 vote of the nine judges. Oksana Baiul skated for a country that had been independent for less than three years.

She was born on November 16, 1977, in Soviet Ukraine, the only child of Sergei and Marina Baiul. Her father left when she was a toddler, and her mother and grandparents raised her. She found skating at about four and was winning by seven. By 13 she had lost her grandparents and her mother. Her longtime coach then moved to Canada, and the coach Galina Zmievskaya took her in to live with her family in Odesa.

She finished 12th at the Soviet championships in 1991. Two years later, at 15, she won the World Championships in Prague, training at what the Christian Science Monitor called an inferior rink. After the Olympics she moved to the United States to skate professionally and settled in Connecticut, where she became a star of American ice shows and television.

By age 13: Had lost her mother and grandparents.
1993: World champion in Prague at 15.

people.name: Alexander Vindman
body: On November 19, 2019, an Army lieutenant colonel in dress uniform testified before the House Intelligence Committee in the impeachment inquiry into President Donald Trump. Alexander Vindman, a National Security Council expert on Ukraine, said the president's July 25, 2019, phone call with Ukraine's new president was improper.

Vindman was born in Kyiv in 1975. In 1979 his father brought him and his twin brother Eugene to the United States as refugees. They arrived in Brooklyn with about $750 and settled in Brighton Beach, a neighborhood of Soviet emigrants.

He was commissioned as an Army infantry officer in 1999 and was wounded by a roadside bomb in Iraq in 2004, receiving the Purple Heart. He became a specialist in Eurasian affairs, with postings at the U.S. embassies in Ukraine and Russia, and joined the National Security Council in 2018.

On February 7, 2020, days after the Senate acquitted the president, he was escorted from the White House and reassigned. He retired from the Army that July after 21 years, saying he had faced bullying and retaliation. He wrote a memoir, Here, Right Matters. He ran for the U.S. Senate from Florida as a Democrat in 2026 and lost the primary to Angie Nixon on August 18. As of October 2026 his brother Eugene represents Virginia's Seventh District in Congress.

1979: Arrived in Brooklyn as a refugee.
1999: Commissioned as an Army infantry officer.
2004: Wounded in Iraq; Purple Heart.
November 2019: Testified in the House impeachment inquiry.
July 2020: Retired from the Army after 21 years.
August 18, 2026: Lost the Florida Democratic Senate primary.

people.name: Natalie Jaresko
body: In March 2017, the federal oversight board created to help Puerto Rico restore fiscal responsibility chose as its executive director a woman who had just served as Ukraine's Minister of Finance in the middle of war and economic collapse. Natalie Jaresko was born in the United States to a family of Ukrainian immigrants.

She earned an accounting degree at DePaul University in Chicago in 1987, became a certified public accountant, and received a master's in public policy from Harvard in 1989. She held economic positions at the State Department and from 1992 to 1995 was chief of the economic section at the new U.S. Embassy in Ukraine. She then spent about two decades investing in businesses in the region, leading the Western NIS Enterprise Fund and co-founding the investment firm Horizon Capital.

On December 2, 2014, President Petro Poroshenko granted her Ukrainian citizenship and parliament confirmed her as finance minister, a post she held into 2016. By her biography for the Yalta European Strategy, she led the negotiation of the largest IMF program to that point and restructured the country's sovereign debt. In Puerto Rico, the board's chairman called her the principal negotiator of the debt restructuring. After a federal judge approved the plan, she announced she would step down effective April 1, 2022.

1989: Master's in public policy, Harvard.
1992–1995: U.S. Embassy in Ukraine.
December 2, 2014: Granted Ukrainian citizenship and confirmed as finance minister.
March 2017–April 2022: Executive director, Puerto Rico's Financial Oversight and Management Board.
people.connectToWork: A person can hold deep ties and duties in two countries at once. Where does your work treat that as a question of loyalty or a complication, rather than as a part of their life?

people.name: Oksana Masters
body: Oksana Masters was born in 1989 in Khmelnytskyi, western Ukraine. She was born with tibial hemimelia, which left her legs different lengths, along with webbed fingers, no thumbs, extra toes and one kidney. The Associated Press reported in 2016 that doctors believe her birth mother was exposed to radiation from the Chornobyl disaster. She spent her first seven and a half years moving among three orphanages. "I wasn't supposed to make it out of the orphanage," she told the AP.

Gay Masters, a speech pathologist in Buffalo, New York, saw her photo and adopted her. A Ukrainian moratorium on foreign adoptions delayed it by about two and a half years. Doctors amputated Oksana's left leg near the knee at nine and her right leg about five years later. The family later moved to Louisville, Kentucky. "My mom literally saved my life," she has said.

She began adaptive rowing at 13 and won a Paralympic bronze in London in 2012, then moved to cross-country skiing, biathlon and cycling. At the Milano Cortina Games in March 2026 she won five medals, four of them gold, bringing her total to 24 across what she calls her eighth Games. The University of Illinois, where she trains, calls her the most decorated Winter Paralympian in U.S. history.
At the 2024 Paris Games she told CNN that an official at the start ramp told her to cover the Ukrainian heart stickers on her helmet. She has written a memoir, The Hard Parts.
keyFacts: 1989: Born in Khmelnytskyi.
To age 7½: Lived in three orphanages.
Adopted by Gay Masters of Buffalo, New York.
Age 9 and about 14: Leg amputations.
2012: First Paralympic medal, rowing.
March 2026: Five medals at Milano Cortina, for 24 in all.
people.connectToWork: Someone who grew up in an institution may have few records and strong views about where care happens. How would you ask what they want from support, without assuming either?

people.name: Iryna Sergiyenko
body: Iryna Sergiyenko's mother, Inna, founded Child With Future in Kyiv in 2011 after Iryna's younger brother Misha was diagnosed with autism. By the family's account, doctors in Ukraine first called his differences just a phase, and the diagnosis came in Israel. Back in Kyiv they found no suitable services.

In March 2022, Iryna, then 30 and by the organization's June 2022 account its director, fled Kyiv with Misha, then 15. Their father could not leave and their grandmother could not travel. They went through Hungary and France to Oxfordshire, England, where she became his sole caregiver.

From there she helped dozens of displaced families with autistic and disabled members find services. She started a Facebook group that had almost 4,000 members in June 2022, linking families to autism organizations and helping specialists who had fled find work. She has argued that refugees may need specialists who understand both trauma and autism. "They're just as traumatized as the rest of us," she said.
keyFacts: 2011: Her mother founded Child With Future.
March 2022: Fled Ukraine with her brother and became his sole caregiver.
June 2022: Her support group had almost 4,000 members.
people.connectToWork: If a behavior changed after a person fled a war, how would your team tell whether a support plan is treating the disability, the trauma, or both?

sources.label: Child With Future / Visable Stories, "She fled the war in Ukraine with her autistic brother" (June 2022)
Child With Future, "How Inna Sergiyenko Built Ukraine's Autism Movement"

institutions.name: St. Constantine Ukrainian Catholic Church
institutions.type: Place of worship and community center
body: Ukrainian immigrants settling in Northeast Minneapolis in the early 1900s found work in the mills and lived where rents were low. In 1913 they founded St. Constantine Ukrainian Catholic Church and built a church at Sixth and University avenues. The parish still stands at 515 University Avenue Northeast and describes itself as serving the Twin Cities since 1913.

Ukrainian Catholics are also called Greek Catholics. The parish's main service is the Divine Liturgy, which it also streams, and it welcomes Catholics of any background. In the 1930s it hosted a ballet class, a drama club, a Ukrainian chorus and the Society of St. Mary, and in 1956 it broke ground for a parochial school. It now holds a Ukrainian Festival, pyrohy (dumpling) sales, a Palm Sunday dinner and a vehicle blessing.

RISU, the Religious Information Service of Ukraine, reports that the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church was banned in Ukraine under Stalin in 1946, that its bishops were sent to labor camps, and that it survived underground until it was legalized in 1989.
keyFacts: 1913: Parish founded.
1930s: Ballet class, drama club, chorus and the Society of St. Mary.
1956: Ground broken for a parochial school.
Today: Divine Liturgy, livestreams, festival and pyrohy sales.
institutions.connectToWork: If a parish could help a newcomer reach your service, how would you ask whether the person wants that connection, and how would you keep the choice theirs?

sources.label: RISU, "Ukraine's forbidden Church marks 25 years of freedom"

institutions.name: Ukrainian American Community Center
aliases: Ukrainian American Community Center of Minnesota
institutions.type: Community center, refugee services, cultural programs
body: In 1964, Dmytro Mandybur, a community leader from the village of Pidhajci who had already founded a Ukrainian credit union, organized a gathering place for Ukrainians in Minneapolis, first called the Ukrainian-American Home. It is now the Ukrainian American Community Center, near the Mississippi riverfront in the old heart of the city's Ukrainian neighborhood.

The center hosts meetings, holiday events and commemorations, including a 2018 event recognizing survivors of the Holodomor, the Soviet-era famine. Since 2006 it has been the site of the Ukrainian Festival of Minnesota. The festival was postponed in 2026 while the center undergoes a major renovation, and it is planned for September 17 and 18, 2027. Its calendar also includes a holiday bazaar, pysanky classes and a Lenten fish fry.

It now describes refugee services among its main work, including a Family Resource Connector, Family Education Mentors, a long-term care workforce program and seminars on visa status, work permits, health insurance and finding medical providers. International Institute of Minnesota classes for new arrivals met there in 2023. CBS Minnesota reported in March 2023 that the center had become a "healing zone" for more than 50 wounded Ukrainian soldiers who came to Minnesota for prosthetics, and FOX 9 reported in 2022 that it had raised $750,000 in humanitarian aid.
keyFacts: 1964: Organized by Dmytro Mandybur as the Ukrainian-American Home.
2006: Became the site of the Ukrainian Festival of Minnesota.
2018: Hosted a Holodomor survivors commemoration.
2023: More than 50 wounded soldiers in Minnesota for prosthetics, CBS Minnesota reported.
2026: Festival postponed during a major renovation.
institutions.connectToWork: Before you refer someone to a community center, what do you need to know about its capacity, and who pays for the work your referral adds?

sources.label: Ukrainian American Community Center, Ukrainian Festival of Minnesota

institutions.name: The Ukrainian Museum
body: On October 3, 1976, the Ukrainian Museum opened in New York City, founded by the Ukrainian National Women's League of America. Its collection began in 1933, when the league bought 600 folk art items for the Ukrainian pavilion at the Chicago World's Fair. After World War II the league resolved to build a museum, and a nationwide fundraising campaign followed.

The museum stands in Manhattan's East Village, long known as Little Ukraine. According to the public history site Clio, it moved into its current building in 2005, designed by the Ukrainian American architect George Sawicki.

It reports holding more than 8,000 folk art objects, 3,300 fine art works and 35,000 archival items, including photographs and letters that document Ukrainian immigration to the United States. After Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 it began the SAFE initiative to support museums and cultural workers in Ukraine. It is marking its 50th anniversary in 2026.
keyFacts: 1933: Collection began with 600 folk art items.
October 3, 1976: Opened in New York.
2005: Moved into its current building.
Holdings: folk art, fine art and immigration archives.
2026: 50th anniversary.
institutions.connectToWork: Whose records would you consult to understand the history of a group you serve, if official records left them out or got them wrong?

sources.label: Ukrainian National Women's League of America, The Ukrainian Museum

institutions.name: Child With Future
body: Child With Future is a Kyiv-based nonprofit founded in 2011 by Inna Sergiyenko after her son's autism diagnosis. Around 2013 she began giving autism lectures across Ukraine and helped parents set up local organizations. By its own account it helped build a preschool model that combines education with specialist support, and it worked to change inclusion policies that first left autistic people out.

It moved outreach online in 2019, began the International Practical Autism Conference that year and kept running online events during the war. After 2022 it helped refugee families with autistic members across Europe. It has no Minnesota office; everything here comes from the organization's own pages.
keyFacts: 2011: Founded in Kyiv.
About 2013: Autism lectures across Ukraine begin.
2019: First International Practical Autism Conference.
2022 on: Support for displaced families.
institutions.connectToWork: Has the person or family used a parent group or service before coming here? How would you find out what worked for them, and build on it?

sources.label: Child With Future, "How Inna Sergiyenko Built Ukraine's Autism Movement"
Child With Future / Visable Stories, "She fled the war in Ukraine with her autistic brother" (June 2022)

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Ukrainian means people who trace their birth or family to Ukraine, from long-settled Northeast Minneapolis families to people who arrived after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. They differ in language, faith, age, generation and experience of war. This review did not find a peer-reviewed U.S. study of how Ukrainian families understand disability, or any Minnesota study. What follows draws on one U.S. refugee study that is not about disability, reporting from Ukraine, and one Ukrainian autism organization's own accounts.
questions: Which language would you like us to use: Ukrainian, Russian or English? Would you like an interpreter even if you speak some English?
What words do you use for what's going on, for you or your family member?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label, here or in another country? Has it helped or got in the way?
What do you want a label or an assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Do you have records from Ukraine or elsewhere that you want us to look at? Is anything missing, or described differently from here?
Who lives with you now, and who is still in Ukraine or somewhere else? Who helps with care?
Who do you want involved in decisions, and who do you not want involved?
Do you have any worries about what disability services would mean for where you or your family member lives? What would you want to know?
Do you have questions about how using services relates to your immigration status? Would you like us to connect you with immigration legal help?
Is a parish, a community center or a parent group important to you? Would you like it included in planning?
Are there things from the war or from leaving that you want your support team to understand? How would you like us to ask about them?
Is there anything about what caused this that you want us to know? You don't have to say.

context.heading: What one U.S. study of Ukrainian refugees reports
body: Childress and colleagues interviewed 32 Ukrainian refugees in the United States, focusing on families with children, in a study published in 2025. They describe five themes: displacement, family separation and trauma before migrating; mental health and well-being; language barriers; conflict over gender roles linked to work; and adjusting to schools, health care, transportation and social assistance. The study is small, is not about disability and did not sample Minnesota.

The authors recommend clarifying future visa status, easy access to English classes and translation tools, and more community-based and remote mental health services. Check these system explanations first when an appointment or a plan is not working.

sources.label: Childress and colleagues, Children and Youth Services Review (2025)

context.heading: Reporting on disability systems in Ukraine
body: These are journalists' accounts of a system, not studies of what families think. In a 2015 article in Euromaidan Press, Olena Makarenko writes that Ukraine inherited a Soviet approach based in state institutions, and she cites the title of a book published in London in 1986 by Valeriy Feofalov, There are no invalids in the USSR! Anna Romandash reports in the Kyiv Post that more than 40,000 Ukrainians lived in institutions when the full-scale invasion began in 2022, including children, older people and mostly people with disabilities. She reports that Ukraine ratified the UN disability rights convention in 2009, and that change has reached mainly children's homes.

This does not tell you how any person feels about services. Someone may have experience of institutions, may have taken part in parent-led inclusion work, or may have neither. If it seems useful, explain plainly that the goal of Minnesota's services is support at home and in the community, and say what is and is not available.

sources.label: Romandash, "(No More) Places of Unfreedom," Kyiv Post

context.heading: Words and documents
body: In the same 2015 article, one person interviewed, Kateryna Smirnova, said "disabled" sounds off-putting and that "handicapped" and "invalid" are worse, and she suggested "people with mobility or other limitations." That is one person's view from 2015. Current official Ukrainian terminology could not be found.

Older documents may use words a person dislikes. Do not repeat a term just because it is on a document. Use a professional interpreter, not a child or the person being served, and have records translated. Explain terms such as waiver, case manager and IEP the first time you use them.

context.heading: Parent-led work and trauma
body: Child With Future, a Kyiv autism organization, reports that one family was told their son's differences were just a phase and got a diagnosis in Israel. Do not assume a person arrives with a diagnosis, or that it matches U.S. categories. These are the organization's own accounts of one family.

The organization's director in 2022, Iryna Sergiyenko, said refugee therapists had treated a new behavior as autism when it had begun after the family fled, and that this was not working. She called for trauma specialists who know autism. The Facebook group she started had almost 4,000 members in June 2022, a sign of the peer networks a person may already use. Ask whether they have one.

context.heading: Immigration status and getting services
body: The Minnesota Department of Health's guidance, last updated in 2024, lists several routes people from Ukraine have used: Uniting for Ukraine sponsorship, humanitarian parole, Temporary Protected Status and Lautenberg refugee admissions. Rules have changed and may change again. Do not guess about status. Refer to immigration legal help.

Worry that using a service could affect status is a reasonable thing to ask about, though no study was found showing it for this group. MPR News reported in February 2023 that more than 900 Ukrainians who had arrived since March 2022 had used federally funded services, by state enrollment counts, and noted that many more may not have used any support services. Do not treat that count as the number of people who need help.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Health, Ukrainian Clinical Guidance (updated September 26, 2024)
Childress and colleagues, Children and Youth Services Review (2025)

context.heading: What could not be found
body: No research was found on faith-based explanations of disability or on traditional healing among Ukrainians in the United States, so nothing is said here about either. No Minnesota organization was found that specifically serves Ukrainian disabled people or families. The Protez Foundation (https://www.protezfoundation.org/), a Minnesota-founded nonprofit, provides prosthetics to Ukrainians with war-related limb loss. The community center and parishes on this page are general community organizations.

communityRoutes.name: Ukrainian American Community Center, Family Resource Connector
communityRoutes.purpose: Helps newly arrived Ukrainian families find services that meet their needs. The center also runs seminars on visa status, work permits, health insurance and finding medical providers. It is not a disability agency, so ask what it can take on.

communityRoutes.name: International Institute of Minnesota
communityRoutes.purpose: St. Paul agency offering refugee services, English classes, citizenship and immigration help, and MNsure assistance. It taught orientation classes for Ukrainian arrivals in 2023.

communityRoutes.name: Minnesota Department of Health, Ukrainian Clinical Guidance
communityRoutes.purpose: Guidance for clinicians, with links to health information in Ukrainian and help translating vaccination records. Last updated in September 2024.

communityRoutes.name: Child With Future
communityRoutes.purpose: Kyiv autism organization with information and online events in Ukrainian. It has no Minnesota office. A family may already know it, so ask.

organizations.intro: MNopedia dates the Ukrainian community of Minneapolis to the late 1870s. Its anchors include St. Constantine (1913), St. Michael's (1925) and the Ukrainian American Community Center (1964). MNopedia lists the records of the Minnesota branch of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America as 1949–1986. Counts of recent arrivals differ because they measure different things. CBS Minnesota reported more than 15,000 Ukrainian refugees in Minnesota in March 2023, without giving its source. MPR News a month earlier cited more than 900 arrivals since March 2022 who had used federally funded services, by state enrollments, and more than 2,700 Uniting for Ukraine applications filed by people in Minnesota. None of these is a census. The list below is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: St. Michael's and St. George's Ukrainian Orthodox Church
entries.purpose: A Ukrainian Orthodox parish, formed in 1925 and in its building since 1926. Holds Divine Liturgy every Sunday at 10 a.m. and memorial services. Its site does not state a liturgical language, but its notices are posted in both Ukrainian and English, and it says longtime members worship alongside recent immigrants. The priest is Fr. Myron Korostil.

entries.name: Cheremosh Ukrainian Dance Ensemble
entries.purpose: Teaches and performs traditional folk dances from regions of Ukraine, for dancers from about age 4 to 24. Part of the Ukrainian American Youth Association. Registration for 2026–2027 is open.

entries.name: Ukrainian Festival MN
entries.purpose: Runs the free annual Ukrainian Festival of Minnesota. Postponed in 2026 during the community center renovation, and planned for September 17 and 18, 2027.

entries.name: Stand With Ukraine MN
entries.purpose: A humanitarian project based at the Ukrainian American Community Center. Its own site reports its fundraising and aid delivery, including $1,198,680.75 raised, with figures last dated September 2025.

entries.name: Plast Minneapolis
entries.purpose: The local branch of Plast, the Ukrainian scouting organization. The community center’s site links to its Facebook page. Ask the center about current meeting times.

entries.name: International Institute of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Offers refugee services, English classes, citizenship and immigration help, job training and MNsure assistance. KSTP reported in July 2022 that it was serving close to 100 Ukrainians and using its Refugee Family Fund for housing and rent.

entries.name: Alight
entries.purpose: A humanitarian agency with hubs in Minneapolis and Nairobi. It lists Poland and Ukraine among the countries where it works, and describes emergency funds and care kits for refugee families in Minnesota.

entries.name: Lutheran Social Service of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Runs refugee services. FOX 9 named it in August 2022 among local agencies to support for Ukrainian refugee housing. Ask about current Ukrainian programs.

entries.name: Arrive Ministries
entries.purpose: A Christian nonprofit working with local churches. Offers resettlement, housing, employment, classes and immigration legal services. FOX 9 named it in August 2022 among local agencies to support for Ukrainian refugee housing.

entries.name: Minnesota Council of Churches
entries.purpose: Its Refugee and Immigrant Services program welcomes and supports newcomers. FOX 9 named it in August 2022 among local agencies to support for Ukrainian refugee housing.

entries.name: Ukrainian Gift Shop
entries.purpose: The Procai and Perchyshyn family business, open since 1947. Sells pysanky supplies, kits and books, mostly by mail and online. It has no walk-in showroom; pickup can be arranged.

entries.name: Kramarczuk's
entries.purpose: The sausage company and deli started by Wasyl and Anna Kramarczuk.

entries.name: Zerkalo
entries.purpose: Publishes the Zerkalo magazine and the North Star community newspaper, mainly in Russian. CCX Media reported in February 2023 on how the publisher keeps Russian-speaking immigrants informed about Ukraine. Do not assume Russian is the language a person wants.

entries.name: Ukrainian American Community Center news page
entries.purpose: Announcements of the center’s seminars, services and events. Its dated news posts can lag behind its programs.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: Nonprofit newsroom covering Minnesota immigrants, including humanitarian parole and Ukrainian newcomers. The link goes to its parole coverage.
entries.linkLabel: Sahan Journal coverage of humanitarian parole

entries.name: KSTP
entries.purpose: Reported in July 2022 on Ukrainian arrivals in Minnesota. The link goes to that story.

entries.name: CBS Minnesota
entries.purpose: Has covered the Ukrainian American Community Center and refugees in Minnesota. The link goes to its March 2023 story.

entries.name: FOX 9
entries.purpose: Reported in August 2022 on what Ukrainian refugees in Minnesota still needed. The link goes to that story.

entries.name: MPR News
entries.purpose: Reported in February 2023 on Ukrainian newcomers one year after fleeing. The link goes to that story.

entries.name: Ukrainian Congress Committee of America
entries.location: New York, with a Washington bureau
entries.purpose: A nonpartisan umbrella group that has represented Ukrainians in the United States since 1940, uniting 30 national organizations and local volunteer chapters. Organizes Ukrainian Days advocacy in Washington.

entries.name: Ukrainian National Women's League of America
entries.purpose: Founded in 1925. Describes itself as the longest-running and largest Ukrainian women’s organization in the U.S. It founded the Ukrainian Museum.

entries.name: Razom
entries.purpose: Programs cover frontline medics, surgery, mental health, veteran care, recovery, advocacy and culture. Its site reports 48 Ukrainians with new prostheses through one program.

entries.name: Nova Ukraine
entries.purpose: Medical aid, rebuilding, psychosocial support, adaptive sports and advocacy, plus housing and resettlement help for Ukrainian refugees in the U.S.

entries.name: United Ukrainian American Relief Committee
entries.purpose: A volunteer-run charity founded in 1944. Ships food and medicine, runs Wheelchairs for Ukraine, and offers citizenship classes and an assistance committee for new U.S. arrivals.

entries.name: Ukrainian National Association
entries.location: Branches across the U.S. and Canada
entries.purpose: Founded in 1894 by Ukrainian immigrants working in Pennsylvania coal mines. Offers life insurance and annuities, funds community projects, and publishes Svoboda and The Ukrainian Weekly.

entries.name: The Ukrainian Weekly
entries.purpose: Founded in 1933. The English-language publication of the Ukrainian National Association.

entries.name: Svoboda
entries.purpose: Founded in 1893. The Ukrainian-language newspaper of the Ukrainian National Association.

entries.name: Ukrainska Pravda
entries.type: International online news; Ukrainian, Russian, English
entries.purpose: Established in 2000 by Georgiy Gongadze.

entries.name: The Kyiv Independent
entries.purpose: Covers Ukraine and Eastern Europe, including war, politics, business and culture.

entries.name: Hromadske
entries.purpose: Covers war, politics, economy and society, with an English edition.

entries.name: Radio Svoboda
entries.type: International radio and online news, Ukrainian
entries.purpose: The Ukrainian-language service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

entries.name: Suspilne
entries.purpose: Ukraine’s public broadcaster and a member of the European Broadcasting Union. Its 2025 award and wartime reporting are described in the linked article.
